reminder: A dihedral angle is the angle between two [half-planes](c:half-plane) that meet along a common line.
definition: Let two [half-planes](c:half-plane) share a boundary line $\ell$. Their dihedral angle is the [angle](c:angle) between two rays that start at one point of $\ell$, lie in the two half-planes, and are perpendicular to $\ell$. For a [convex polyhedron](c:convex-polyhedron), the dihedral angle at an [edge](c:edge) is the angle between the two [faces](c:face) that meet there, measured inside the polyhedron.
examples: In a cube, every dihedral angle between two adjacent faces is $\pi/2$.
In a regular tetrahedron, every dihedral angle is $\arccos(1/3)$, about $70.5^\circ$.
Non-example: the angle between two edges at one vertex of a face lies in a single plane, so it is a plane angle and not a dihedral angle.

reminder: A vector is diophantine when nonzero integer combinations of its entries never come closer to zero than a fixed power of their size allows.
definition: A vector $\omega=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_n)$ of [real numbers](c:real-number) satisfies a diophantine condition when there are constants $\gamma>0$ and $\tau\ge n-1$ with $|k\cdot\omega|\ge\gamma|k|^{-\tau}$ for every nonzero [integer](c:integer) vector $k$. The condition keeps $\omega$ far from every [rational](c:rational-number) resonance $k\cdot\omega=0$, which is the assumption on the frequencies of a motion on a [torus](c:torus) in Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser theory.
examples: The vector $(1,\sqrt2)$ is diophantine: $|k_1+k_2\sqrt2|\ge c/|k|$ for all nonzero integer vectors $(k_1,k_2)$.
For each $\tau>n-1$, almost every vector of $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies the condition for some $\gamma>0$.
Non-example: $\omega=(1,2)$ is not diophantine, because $k=(2,-1)$ gives $k\cdot\omega=0$.
Non-example: $(1,\lambda)$ with the Liouville number $\lambda=\sum_{j\ge1}10^{-j!}$ is not diophantine for any $\tau$, because rational numbers approximate $\lambda$ faster than any power.

reminder: A Dirac measure gives a set the value 1 if it contains one fixed [point](c:point), and the value 0 if it does not.
definition: Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) and let $x\in X$. The Dirac [measure](c:measure) at $x$ is $\delta_x(A)=1$ if $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A)=0$ if $x\notin A$, for every measurable set $A$. The [integral](c:integral) of a measurable function $f$ against $\delta_x$ is $f(x)$.
examples: A finite sum $\sum_i p_i\delta_{x_i}$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$ is a discrete probability measure.
Non-example: the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ is not a Dirac measure, because every single point has measure $0$.

steps: Let $\delta_x$ be the Dirac measure at $x$ on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$.
The empty set does not contain $x$, so $\delta_x(\emptyset)=0$.
Disjoint sets contain $x$ in at most one of them, so $\delta_x$ is countably additive.
The whole space contains $x$, so $\delta_x(X)=1$ and $\delta_x$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure).
links.why: It shows that a Dirac measure is the simplest probability measure, with all its mass on one point.

reminder: The direct image $f_*$ of a [geometric morphism](c:geometric-morphism) $f$ is the right [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) of the inverse image $f^*$.
definition: A [geometric morphism](c:geometric-morphism) $f:\mathcal E\to\mathcal F$ of [topoi](c:topos) is a pair of [adjoint functors](c:adjoint-functor) $f^*\dashv f_*$ such that the left adjoint $f^*$ preserves finite limits. The direct image is the right adjoint $f_*:\mathcal E\to\mathcal F$. For a continuous map $g:X\to Y$ and a [sheaf](c:sheaf) $F$ on $X$, it is $(g_*F)(V)=F(g^{-1}(V))$ for every open set $V$ of $Y$.
examples: For a continuous map $g:X\to Y$, the sheaf $g_*F$ on $Y$ has the sections $F(g^{-1}(V))$ over an open set $V$.
For the map $X\to\mathrm{pt}$, the direct image sends a sheaf $F$ to its set of global sections $F(X)$.
Non-example: the inverse image $f^*$ is the left adjoint of $f_*$, so it is not the direct image.

steps: Take a geometric morphism $f$ with its pair $f^*\dashv f_*$.
The pair is an adjunction, so $f_*$ is the right adjoint in an [adjoint functor](c:adjoint-functor) pair.
The geometric case adds that the left adjoint $f^*$ preserves finite limits.
links.why: It shows that direct images have every property of right adjoints, such as preserving limits.

steps: Let $\mathcal E$ be a [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos) with its unique geometric morphism $\gamma:\mathcal E\to\mathbf{Set}$.
The direct image $\gamma_*$ sends an object $F$ to the set $\mathrm{Hom}(1,F)$ of maps from the terminal object.
That set is the set of [global sections](c:global-section) of $F$.
links.why: It shows that taking global sections is the direct image to the topos of sets.

reminder: A Dirichlet character modulo $N$ is a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) from the units modulo $N$ to the nonzero complex numbers.
definition: A Dirichlet character modulo $N$ is a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) $\chi:(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times\to\mathbb{C}^\times$ from the [unit group](c:unit-group) of the integers modulo $N$ ([modular arithmetic](c:modular-arithmetic)) to the nonzero [complex numbers](c:complex-number). One extends it to all integers by $\chi(n)=\chi(n\bmod N)$ when $\gcd(n,N)=1$ and $\chi(n)=0$ otherwise. The extended function is periodic with period $N$ and completely multiplicative.
examples: The principal character modulo $N$ has $\chi(n)=1$ when $\gcd(n,N)=1$ and $\chi(n)=0$ otherwise.
Modulo $4$, $\chi(n)=1$ for $n\equiv1$, $\chi(n)=-1$ for $n\equiv3$, and $\chi(n)=0$ for even $n$.
The Legendre symbol $(n/p)$ is a Dirichlet character modulo an odd prime $p$.
Non-example: $\chi(n)=n\bmod 5$ is not a Dirichlet character, because $\chi(2)\chi(3)=6$ but $\chi(6)=1$.

steps: Take the ring $R=\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ and the complex numbers as the target.
A Dirichlet character is a multiplicative map $R\to\mathbb{C}$ that sends every non-unit of $R$ to $0$.
The non-units of $R$ are the classes of integers not coprime to $N$, which gives the extension rule.
links.why: It shows that a Dirichlet character is a multiplicative character of the ring of integers modulo $N$.

reminder: A Dirichlet distribution is a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on the [simplex](c:simplex) whose density is proportional to $\prod_i x_i^{\alpha_i-1}$.
definition: For parameters $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_K>0$, the Dirichlet distribution $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$ is the [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on the [simplex](c:simplex) $\{x: x_i\ge0,\ \sum_i x_i=1\}$ with [density](c:probability-density-function) $\frac{\Gamma(\sum_i\alpha_i)}{\prod_i\Gamma(\alpha_i)}\prod_i x_i^{\alpha_i-1}$ with respect to Lebesgue measure on the first $K-1$ coordinates. Equivalently, if $G_1,\dots,G_K$ are independent [gamma](c:gamma-distribution) variables with shapes $\alpha_i$, then $(G_1,\dots,G_K)/\sum_jG_j$ has this distribution.
examples: $\mathrm{Dir}(1,\dots,1)$ is the uniform distribution on the simplex.
For $K=2$, the vector $(X,1-X)$ with $X$ beta distributed has a Dirichlet distribution.
The mean of $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$ is $\alpha/\sum_j\alpha_j$.
Non-example: a random vector whose coordinates sum to $2$ is not Dirichlet, because every Dirichlet vector has coordinate sum $1$.

reminder: A Dirichlet eigenvalue of a domain is a number $\lambda$ with $-\Delta u=\lambda u$ for some nonzero $u$ that is zero on the boundary.
definition: Let $\Omega$ be a bounded [open set](c:open-set) in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$. A number $\lambda$ is a Dirichlet [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of $\Omega$ when $-\Delta u=\lambda u$ in $\Omega$ has a solution $u\ne0$ with the Dirichlet [boundary condition](c:boundary-condition) $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, where $\Delta$ is the [Laplace operator](c:laplace-operator). These numbers form a sequence $0<\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots\to\infty$, repeated by multiplicity; the same definition works with the Laplace–Beltrami operator on a Riemannian manifold with boundary.
examples: On the interval $(0,\pi)$, the Dirichlet eigenvalues are $k^2$ for $k=1,2,3,\dots$, with eigenfunctions $\sin kx$.
On the unit square $(0,1)^2$, they are $\pi^2(m^2+n^2)$ for integers $m,n\ge1$.
Non-example: $0$ is not a Dirichlet eigenvalue, because the only solution of $\Delta u=0$ that vanishes on the boundary is $u=0$.

steps: Let $A$ be the operator $-\Delta$ acting on smooth functions on $\Omega$ that vanish on the boundary.
An [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of $A$ is a number $\lambda$ with $Au=\lambda u$ for some nonzero $u$ in its domain.
These numbers are the Dirichlet eigenvalues, so the Dirichlet case adds the boundary condition $u=0$.
links.why: It shows that Dirichlet eigenvalues are ordinary eigenvalues of the Laplace operator on a domain that encodes the boundary condition.

reminder: The discrete Fourier transform sends a list of $N$ numbers to its coefficients in the $N$ complex waves $e^{2\pi ikn/N}$.
definition: For a list $f=(f(0),\dots,f(N-1))$ of [complex numbers](c:complex-number), the discrete Fourier transform is $\hat f(k)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f(n)e^{-2\pi ikn/N}$ for $k=0,\dots,N-1$. It is the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) of a function on the [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, and $e^{2\pi i/N}$ is a primitive $N$th [root of unity](c:root-of-unity).
examples: The transform of the list $(1,0,\dots,0)$ is the constant list $(1,1,\dots,1)$.
The transform of the constant list $(1,\dots,1)$ is $(N,0,\dots,0)$.
Non-example: the Fourier series of a function on the circle has infinitely many coefficients, so it is not a discrete Fourier transform.

steps: On a finite abelian group $G$, the Fourier transform of $f$ is $\hat f(\chi)=\sum_{g\in G}f(g)\overline{\chi(g)}$ over the characters $\chi$.
The characters of $G=\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ are the maps $n\mapsto e^{2\pi ikn/N}$ for $k=0,\dots,N-1$.
With these characters, the sum is exactly $\sum_n f(n)e^{-2\pi ikn/N}$.
So the discrete Fourier transform is the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) for the cyclic group.
links.why: It shows that the discrete transform is the group Fourier transform for a cyclic group, so its rules follow from the general ones.

reminder: The disjoint union of two [sets](c:set) holds a separate copy of each, so shared elements stay apart.
definition: The disjoint union of [sets](c:set) $A$ and $B$ is $A\sqcup B=(\{0\}\times A)\cup(\{1\}\times B)$, with the [functions](c:function) $A\to A\sqcup B$ and $B\to A\sqcup B$ that attach the labels $0$ and $1$. It is the [coproduct](c:coproduct) of $A$ and $B$ in the category of sets. For a family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ one uses $\bigcup_{i\in I}\{i\}\times A_i$.
examples: $\{a,b\}\sqcup\{a,c\}$ has four elements: $(0,a)$, $(0,b)$, $(1,a)$ and $(1,c)$.
For finite sets, $|A\sqcup B|=|A|+|B|$.
Non-example: the union $\{a,b\}\cup\{a,c\}=\{a,b,c\}$ has three elements, because the common element $a$ appears once.

steps: Take [functions](c:function) $f:A\to X$ and $g:B\to X$.
Define $h:A\sqcup B\to X$ by $h(0,a)=f(a)$ and $h(1,b)=g(b)$.
This $h$ is the only function that agrees with $f$ and $g$ on the two copies.
So $A\sqcup B$ with its two injections has the universal property of a [coproduct](c:coproduct) in sets.
links.why: It shows that the disjoint union is the coproduct of sets, so results on coproducts apply to it.

reminder: The distance between two [points](c:point) is the length of the straight line segment that joins them.
definition: In [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$, the distance between points $x$ and $y$ is $d(x,y)=\sqrt{\sum_i(x_i-y_i)^2}$, the length of the [line segment](c:line-segment) from $x$ to $y$. A distance on a general set is a function $d$ with $d(x,y)\ge0$, $d(x,y)=0$ only for $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$, and a set with such a function is a [metric space](c:metric-space).
examples: In the plane, the points $(0,0)$ and $(3,4)$ have distance $5$.
On the real line, the distance is $d(x,y)=|x-y|$.
On a sphere, the length of the shorter great-circle arc between two points is also a distance.
Non-example: $x-y$ is not a distance on $\mathbb{R}$, because it is negative when $x<y$.

reminder: A distributed system is a set of separate computers that work together by sending messages to each other.
definition: A distributed system is a finite set of nodes, such as computers or processes, and each node has its own memory and its own clock. The nodes communicate only by sending messages over links, and the nodes and links form a [graph](c:graph). The nodes run one [algorithm](c:algorithm) together, although messages can be delayed or lost and nodes can fail.
examples: A database that keeps copies of its data on servers in several data centers.
A blockchain network, in which many independent nodes agree on one ledger by exchanging messages.
Non-example: one program with several threads that share the memory of a single computer.

reminder: A distribution of subspaces picks a subspace of fixed dimension in each tangent space of a [manifold](c:smooth-manifold), varying smoothly from point to point.
definition: A distribution of rank $k$ on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ is a choice of a $k$-dimensional linear subspace $D_p\subseteq T_pM$ for every point $p$, such that these subspaces form a smooth subbundle of the [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle). Equivalently, near each point there are $k$ smooth vector fields that are linearly independent and span $D$ at every point; so $D$ is a [real vector bundle](c:real-vector-bundle) of rank $k$ inside $TM$.
examples: A vector field $X$ without zeros gives the rank-1 distribution spanned by $X$.
On $\mathbb{R}^3$, the planes $\ker(dz-y\,dx)$ form a rank-2 distribution, the standard contact structure.
Non-example: on $\mathbb{R}$, the spans of $x\,\partial_x$ do not form a distribution, because the dimension is $0$ at $x=0$ and $1$ elsewhere.

steps: Start with a distribution $D$ on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold).
Add the condition that $D$ is involutive: the Lie bracket of two vector fields in $D$ lies in $D$.
By the Frobenius theorem, such a $D$ is the tangent distribution of a [foliation](c:foliation).
Then $D$ is an [integrable distribution of subspaces](c:integrable-distribution-of-subspaces).
links.why: It shows that integrability is one extra condition on a distribution, the closure under the Lie bracket.

reminder: A [series](c:series) is divergent when its partial sums do not approach a finite limit.
definition: A [series](c:series) $\sum_n a_n$ of numbers is divergent when its partial sums $s_N=\sum_{n\le N}a_n$ do not [converge](c:convergence) to a finite limit. A series of functions is divergent at a point when the series of its values at that point is divergent.
examples: The harmonic series $\sum 1/n$ diverges, because its partial sums grow like $\ln N$.
The series $\sum(-1)^n$ diverges, because its partial sums alternate between $1$ and $0$.
The series $\sum n!\,x^n$ diverges for every $x\ne0$.
Non-example: $\sum 1/n^2$ converges to $\pi^2/6$, so it is not divergent.

reminder: The divisor function $\sigma_k(n)$ adds the $k$-th powers of all positive [divisors](c:divisibility) of $n$.
definition: For an integer $k\ge0$ and a positive [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$, the divisor function is $\sigma_k(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d^k$, where $d$ runs over the positive numbers that divide $n$. For $k=0$ it counts the divisors of $n$, and for $k=1$ it adds them.
examples: $\sigma_1(6)=1+2+3+6=12=2\cdot6$, so $6$ is a perfect number.
$\sigma_0(12)=6$, because $12$ has the divisors $1,2,3,4,6,12$.
For a prime $p$, $\sigma_k(p)=1+p^k$.
Non-example: $\sum_{d\le n}d^k$ is not $\sigma_k(n)$, because it adds all $d\le n$; for $n=6$ and $k=1$ it gives $21$, not $12$.

steps: An [arithmetic function](c:arithmetic-function) is a function defined on the positive integers.
The rule $n\mapsto\sum_{d\mid n}d^k$ gives one value for each positive integer $n$.
So $\sigma_k$ is an arithmetic function, and it is multiplicative: $\sigma_k(mn)=\sigma_k(m)\sigma_k(n)$ when $\gcd(m,n)=1$.
links.why: It shows that $\sigma_k$ is an arithmetic function with the extra property of multiplicativity.

reminder: A dense linear order without endpoints has no first or last element, and between two elements there is always another.
definition: A dense linear order without endpoints is a nonempty set $X$ with a [total order](c:total-order) $<$ such that for every $x$ there are $y,z$ with $y<x<z$, and for all $x<y$ there is $z$ with $x<z<y$ (the order is [dense](c:densely-ordered)). Any two countable such orders are isomorphic (Cantor), so $(\mathbb{Q},<)$ is the model.
examples: $(\mathbb{Q},<)$ and $(\mathbb{R},<)$ are dense linear orders without endpoints.
The open interval $(0,1)$ with its usual order is one too.
Non-example: $(\mathbb{Z},<)$ has no endpoints but is not dense, because no integer lies between $0$ and $1$.
Non-example: $[0,1]$ is dense but has the endpoints $0$ and $1$.

steps: Start with a [dense linear order](c:dense-linear-order) $(X,<)$.
Add the condition that $X$ has no least element.
Add the condition that $X$ has no greatest element.
Then $(X,<)$ is a dense linear order without endpoints.
links.why: It shows that the endpoint-free case needs exactly two more conditions on a dense linear order.

reminder: A double affine Hecke algebra holds two affine [Hecke algebras](c:hecke-algebra) of a [root system](c:is-root-system) that share one finite Hecke subalgebra.
definition: Let $R$ be a [root system](c:is-root-system) with [Weyl group](c:weyl-group) $W$. The double affine Hecke algebra of $R$ is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) over $\mathbb{C}$ with a parameter $q$ and parameters $t_\alpha$ (one for each orbit of roots). It contains the finite [Hecke algebra](c:hecke-algebra) of $W$ and two families of commuting invertible elements $X_b$ and $Y_a$, indexed by a lattice and its dual, so that each family together with the finite Hecke algebra generates an affine Hecke algebra.
examples: In the polynomial representation on Laurent polynomials in the $X_b$, the nonsymmetric Macdonald polynomials are common eigenvectors of the $Y_a$.
The algebra of type $A_{n-1}$ acts on Laurent polynomials in $X_1,\dots,X_n$ by Demazure–Lusztig operators and $q$-shifts.
Non-example: the finite Hecke algebra of $W$ is not a double affine Hecke algebra, because it has no lattice elements $X_b$ or $Y_a$.

reminder: A double complex is a grid of objects with horizontal and vertical [differentials](c:differential) that each square to zero and commute.
definition: A double complex in an [additive category](c:additive-category) is a family of objects $C_{p,q}$ for integers $p,q$, with maps $d^h:C_{p,q}\to C_{p-1,q}$ and $d^v:C_{p,q}\to C_{p,q-1}$ such that $d^hd^h=0$, $d^vd^v=0$ and $d^hd^v=d^vd^h$. Each row and each column is then a [chain complex](c:chain-complex); some authors ask instead that $d^h$ and $d^v$ anticommute.
examples: For chain complexes $A$ and $B$, the objects $C_{p,q}=A_p\otimes B_q$ with $d^h=d_A\otimes1$ and $d^v=1\otimes d_B$ form a double complex.
The Čech–de Rham complex of an open cover is a double complex with the Čech and the de Rham differentials.
Non-example: a grid in which $d^hd^h\ne0$ for some square is not a double complex, because its rows are not chain complexes.

steps: Start with a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $(A_p,d)$.
Put $C_{p,0}=A_p$ and $C_{p,q}=0$ for $q\ne0$.
Take $d^h=d$ and $d^v=0$.
All three identities hold, so $C$ is a double complex with one nonzero row.
links.why: It shows that a chain complex is a double complex with one row, so results on double complexes include chain complexes.

reminder: The double coset $HgK$ of $g$ is the set of all products $hgk$ with $h$ in $H$ and $k$ in $K$.
definition: Let $H$ and $K$ be [subgroups](c:subgroup) of a [group](c:group) $G$. The double coset of $g\in G$ is $HgK=\{hgk: h\in H,\ k\in K\}$. These sets are the orbits of the [action](c:group-action) of $H\times K$ on $G$ by $(h,k)\cdot g=hgk^{-1}$, so they partition $G$, and the set of double cosets is written $H\backslash G/K$.
examples: If $K=\{e\}$, then $HgK=Hg$ is an ordinary right coset of $H$.
In $S_3$ with $H=K=\{e,(12)\}$, there are two double cosets: $H$ itself, of size $2$, and the other four elements.
In $GL_n(k)$ with $B$ the upper triangular matrices, the Bruhat decomposition writes $GL_n(k)$ as the disjoint union of the double cosets $BwB$ for permutation matrices $w$.
Non-example: for $H=K=\{e,(12)\}$ in $S_3$, the set $\{(13),(23)\}$ is not a double coset, because $H(13)K$ has four elements.

steps: Take the double coset $HgK$ of two subgroups $H$ and $K$ of $G$.
Choose $H=\{e\}$, the trivial subgroup.
Then $HgK=gK$, which is a left [coset](c:coset) of $K$.
So every left coset is a double coset.
links.why: It shows that a double coset adds a second subgroup that acts from the other side.

reminder: A Drinfeld associator is a [grouplike](c:grouplike-element) power series in two non-commuting variables that satisfies the pentagon and hexagon equations.
definition: Let $\mathbf{k}$ be a [field](c:field) of characteristic $0$ and let $\lambda\in\mathbf{k}^\times$. A $\lambda$-associator is a [grouplike element](c:grouplike-element) $\Phi(A,B)$ of the algebra of [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) in two non-commuting variables $A,B$, with $\Phi(A,B)\Phi(B,A)=1$, that satisfies two hexagon equations and the pentagon equation. The pentagon equation holds in the completed enveloping algebra of the [Drinfeld–Kohno Lie algebra](c:drinfeld-kohno-lie-algebra) on four strands.
examples: The Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov associator, built from the monodromy of the KZ equation, is an associator over $\mathbb{C}$; its coefficients are multiple zeta values up to powers of $2\pi i$.
Drinfeld proved that associators exist over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Non-example: $\Phi=1$ is grouplike and satisfies the pentagon equation, but it fails the hexagon equations, because $A$ and $B$ do not commute.

reminder: A Drinfeld shtuka is a pair of vector bundles on a curve times a base, joined by two maps, one of them twisted by Frobenius.
definition: Let $X$ be a smooth projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) over a [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_q$ and let $S$ be a [scheme](c:scheme) over $\mathbb{F}_q$. A shtuka of rank $r$ over $S$ is a pair of rank-$r$ [vector bundles](c:vector-bundle) $\mathcal E,\mathcal E'$ on $X\times S$ with maps $j:\mathcal E\to\mathcal E'$ and $t:{}^\tau\mathcal E\to\mathcal E'$, where ${}^\tau\mathcal E$ is the pullback of $\mathcal E$ by the [Frobenius](c:frobenius) of $S$. The maps $j$ and $t$ are injective, and each cokernel is an invertible sheaf on the graph of a morphism $S\to X$, called a leg.
examples: Over a point $S=\operatorname{Spec}k$, a rank-$r$ shtuka is a pair of rank-$r$ bundles on $X_k$ with two injections whose cokernels are skyscraper sheaves of length $1$ at two points.
A Drinfeld module of rank $r$ gives a shtuka of rank $r$ with one leg at the place at infinity.
Non-example: a bundle $\mathcal E$ with an isomorphism $\mathcal E\cong{}^\tau\mathcal E$ has no legs, so it is not a Drinfeld shtuka.

reminder: A du Val singularity is a surface singularity of the form $\mathbb{C}^2/\Gamma$ for a finite subgroup $\Gamma$ of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$.
definition: A du Val singularity, also called a simple surface singularity or rational double point, is a [singularity](c:singularity) isomorphic to the origin of $\mathbb{C}^2/\Gamma$, where $\Gamma$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group) inside the [special linear group](c:special-linear-group) $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$. Equivalently, it is the origin of one of the surfaces $A_n$: $x^2+y^2+z^{n+1}=0$, $D_n$: $x^2+y^2z+z^{n-1}=0$, $E_6$: $x^2+y^3+z^4=0$, $E_7$: $x^2+y^3+yz^3=0$ or $E_8$: $x^2+y^3+z^5=0$ in $\mathbb{C}^3$.
examples: The surface $A_1$: $x^2+y^2+z^2=0$ has the singularity $\mathbb{C}^2/\{\pm1\}$ at the origin.
The surface $E_8$: $x^2+y^3+z^5=0$ has the singularity $\mathbb{C}^2/\Gamma$ at the origin, where $\Gamma$ is the binary icosahedral group of order $120$.
Non-example: $x^2+y^3+z^6=0$ is not du Val, because its singularity at the origin is simple elliptic and not rational.

reminder: The Duflo isomorphism identifies, as algebras, the invariants of the [symmetric algebra](c:symmetric-algebra) with the [center](c:center) of the enveloping algebra.
definition: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over a field of characteristic $0$. The symmetrisation map $\beta:S(\mathfrak g)\to U(\mathfrak g)$ from the [symmetric algebra](c:symmetric-algebra) to the [universal enveloping algebra](c:universal-enveloping-algebra) is an isomorphism of vector spaces, and it maps the invariants $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}$ onto the [center](c:center) $Z(\mathfrak g)$ of $U(\mathfrak g)$. The Duflo isomorphism is $\beta\circ\partial_{j^{1/2}}$, where $\partial_{j^{1/2}}$ is the differential operator with symbol $j^{1/2}$ and $j(x)=\det\frac{1-e^{-\mathrm{ad}\,x}}{\mathrm{ad}\,x}$; it is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) of algebras $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}\to Z(\mathfrak g)$.
examples: For an abelian Lie algebra, $j=1$, and the Duflo isomorphism is the identity of $S(\mathfrak g)=U(\mathfrak g)$.
For the two-dimensional Lie algebra with $[x,y]=y$, both $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}$ and $Z(\mathfrak g)$ consist of the scalars.
Non-example: the symmetrisation map $\beta$ alone is only a linear isomorphism on invariants, and it differs from the Duflo isomorphism whenever $j\ne1$, for example for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$.

reminder: A dyadic rational number is a [rational number](c:rational-number) of the form $m/2^k$ with $m$ an integer and $k\ge0$.
definition: A dyadic rational number is a [rational number](c:rational-number) that can be written as $m/2^k$ with $m$ an [integer](c:integer) and $k$ a [natural number](c:natural-number). Equivalently, its binary expansion has finitely many digits.
examples: $3/8=0.011_2$ is dyadic, and so is every integer (take $k=0$).
Non-example: $1/3=0.010101\ldots_2$ is not dyadic, because its binary expansion never ends.

steps: Take a dyadic rational number $m/2^k$.
It is a quotient of the integers $m$ and $2^k$ with $2^k\ne0$, so it is a [rational number](c:rational-number).
The dyadic case adds the condition that the denominator is a power of $2$.
links.why: It shows that dyadic rationals are the rational numbers whose denominator is a power of two.

reminder: The number $e$ is the base of the natural [logarithm](c:logarithm), and the [exponential function](c:exponential-function) $e^x$ is its own derivative.
definition: The number $e=\sum_{n=0}^\infty 1/n!=\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+1/n)^n\approx2.71828$ is the unique base $b>0$ for which $b^x$ has [derivative](c:derivative) $1$ at $x=0$, so that $\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x$. The natural [logarithm](c:logarithm) $\ln$ is the inverse of $x\mapsto e^x$, and $e$ is an [irrational number](c:irrational-number) given by a convergent [series](c:series).
examples: $e=1+1+\tfrac12+\tfrac16+\tfrac1{24}+\cdots$, so $e\approx2.71828$.
With interest rate $100\%$ compounded $n$ times a year, one unit grows to $(1+1/n)^n$ after one year, and this tends to $e$.
Non-example: the decimal $2.71828$ is not $e$, because $e$ is irrational and no finite decimal equals it.

reminder: An ear decomposition builds a [graph](c:graph) from one [cycle](c:cycle) by adding paths, called ears, whose end points already lie in the built graph.
definition: An ear decomposition of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ is a sequence $P_0,P_1,\dots,P_k$ of subgraphs whose edge sets partition the edges of $G$. Here $P_0$ is a [cycle](c:cycle), and each later ear $P_i$ is a [path](c:path) or a cycle whose end vertices (or single attaching vertex, for a cycle) lie in $P_0\cup\dots\cup P_{i-1}$ while its other vertices do not. A connected graph with an edge has an ear decomposition exactly when it has no bridge (Robbins).
examples: In the complete graph $K_4$ on $a,b,c,d$, take $P_0$ the triangle $abc$, $P_1$ the path $a\,d\,b$, and $P_2$ the edge $cd$.
A cycle graph is its own ear decomposition, with $k=0$.
Non-example: two triangles joined by one edge have no ear decomposition, because the joining edge is a bridge and lies on no cycle.
Non-example: a tree with an edge has no ear decomposition, because it has no cycle to start with.

reminder: An edge coloring of a [graph](c:graph) gives each edge one color from a fixed set of colors.
definition: An edge coloring of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ with a set $C$ of colors is a [function](c:function) $c:E(G)\to C$ that gives each edge a color; it is proper when edges that share a vertex have different colors. A subgraph is monochromatic when all its edges have the same color, and Ramsey theory looks for monochromatic [complete subgraphs](c:complete-graph) in colorings of complete graphs.
examples: Color the edges of $K_5$ red on the outer $5$-cycle and blue on the inner $5$-cycle; this coloring has no monochromatic triangle.
A cycle with four edges has a proper edge coloring with two colors: color the edges alternately.
Non-example: a rule that gives colors to the vertices of a graph is a vertex coloring, not an edge coloring.

reminder: An effective action is the [action functional](c:action-functional) that remains after one integrates out some fields or modes of a more fundamental action.
definition: Let $S[\phi,\chi]$ be an [action functional](c:action-functional) of a field $\phi$ and further fields $\chi$. The effective action $S_{\mathrm{eff}}[\phi]$ is defined by $e^{iS_{\mathrm{eff}}[\phi]/\hbar}=\int e^{iS[\phi,\chi]/\hbar}\,D\chi$, so it averages out the dependence on $\chi$ in a [path integral](c:path-integral). In perturbation theory it is a sum over connected [Feynman diagrams](c:feynman-diagram) whose internal lines are $\chi$ lines.
examples: At tree level, $S_{\mathrm{eff}}[\phi]=S[\phi,\chi_{\mathrm{cl}}(\phi)]$, where $\chi_{\mathrm{cl}}(\phi)$ solves the equation of motion for $\chi$.
Integrating out the electron field in quantum electrodynamics leaves an effective action for the photon, with the Euler–Heisenberg self-interaction.
Wilsonian [renormalization](c:renormalization) integrates out the high-energy modes of a field and leaves an effective action for the low-energy modes.
Non-example: the classical action $S[\phi]$ itself is not an effective action, because no field has been integrated out.

reminder: The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios that no other portfolio beats on both expected return and variance.
definition: Consider $n$ risky assets with expected return vector $\mu$ and [covariance matrix](c:covariance-matrix) $\Sigma$, and a portfolio $w$ with $\sum_iw_i=1$. Its [expected value](c:expected-value) of return is $\mu^\top w$ and its [variance](c:variance) is $w^\top\Sigma w$. The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios $w$ such that no other portfolio $w'$ has $\mu^\top w'\ge\mu^\top w$ and $w'^\top\Sigma w'\le w^\top\Sigma w$ with at least one inequality strict.
examples: For two risky assets with correlation different from $\pm1$, the minimum-variance portfolios form a hyperbola branch in the plane of standard deviation and expected return, and the efficient frontier is its upper half, starting at the minimum-variance portfolio.
Adding a risk-free asset turns the frontier into a straight line, the capital market line, that touches the old frontier at the tangency portfolio.
Non-example: a portfolio on the lower half of the hyperbola is not efficient, because another portfolio with the same variance has a higher expected return.

reminder: An Eilenberg–Mac Lane space $K(G,n)$ has the group $G$ as its $n$-th [homotopy group](c:homotopy-group) and all other homotopy groups zero.
definition: Let $n\ge1$ and let $G$ be a group, which is [abelian](c:abelian-group) when $n\ge2$. A space $K(G,n)$ is a [connected](c:connected-space) [topological space](c:topological-space), usually taken to be a [CW complex](c:cw-complex), with [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) $\pi_n\cong G$ and $\pi_k=0$ for all $k\ne n$. Any two such CW complexes are homotopy equivalent.
examples: The circle $S^1$ is a $K(\mathbb{Z},1)$, because its universal cover $\mathbb{R}$ is contractible.
The space $\mathbb{RP}^\infty$ is a $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)$, and $\mathbb{CP}^\infty$ is a $K(\mathbb{Z},2)$.
Non-example: $S^2$ is not a $K(\mathbb{Z},2)$, because $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}$ is not zero.

steps: Take a discrete group $G$ and its [classifying space](c:classifying-space) $BG$.
The space $BG$ is connected and $\pi_1(BG)\cong G$.
Its universal cover is contractible, so $\pi_k(BG)=0$ for $k\ge2$.
So $BG$ is a $K(G,1)$, the case $n=1$ of an Eilenberg–Mac Lane space.
links.why: It shows that the classifying space of a group is the first level of the Eilenberg–Mac Lane family.

reminder: The Eilenberg–Moore category of a [monad](c:monad) $T$ has the $T$-algebras as objects and the structure-preserving maps as morphisms.
definition: Let $(T,\eta,\mu)$ be a [monad](c:monad) on a [category](c:category) $\mathcal C$. A $T$-algebra is an object $A$ with a morphism $a:TA\to A$ such that $a\circ\eta_A=\mathrm{id}_A$ and $a\circ Ta=a\circ\mu_A$. The Eilenberg–Moore category $\mathcal C^T$ has these algebras as objects, and its morphisms $(A,a)\to(B,b)$ are the morphisms $f:A\to B$ of $\mathcal C$ with $f\circ a=b\circ Tf$.
examples: For the free group monad on sets, the Eilenberg–Moore category is the category of groups.
For the power set monad on sets, the algebras are complete lattices, and the morphisms are the maps that preserve all joins.
Non-example: for the list monad on sets, take $A=\{0,1\}$ and $a(w)=0$ for every list $w$; this pair is not an algebra, because $a([1])=0\ne1$ breaks the unit law.

steps: Let $T$ be a monad, so $T$ is also an [endofunctor](c:endofunctor).
Every $T$-algebra $a:TA\to A$ is then an [algebra for the endofunctor](c:algebra-for-an-endofunctor) $T$.
The Eilenberg–Moore case adds two laws on $a$: the unit law and the associativity law.
The morphisms are the same in both categories, so the Eilenberg–Moore category is a full subcategory.
links.why: It shows that an algebra of a monad is an algebra of its endofunctor that also obeys the two monad laws.

reminder: An Einstein metric is a Riemannian metric whose [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) is a constant multiple of the metric.
definition: A [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $(M,g)$ of dimension $n$ is Einstein, and $g$ is an Einstein metric, when the [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) satisfies $\mathrm{Ric}(g)=\lambda g$ for a constant $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$. Taking the trace gives $\lambda=\mathrm{scal}/n$, so the scalar curvature is constant.
examples: The unit round sphere $S^n$ has $\mathrm{Ric}=(n-1)g$.
Flat $\mathbb{R}^n$ has $\mathrm{Ric}=0$, and hyperbolic space has $\mathrm{Ric}=-(n-1)g$.
Calabi–Yau metrics on compact Kähler manifolds are Ricci-flat, so they are Einstein with $\lambda=0$.
Non-example: the product of a unit $2$-sphere and a $2$-sphere of radius $2$ has $\mathrm{Ric}=g_1\oplus\frac14g_2$, so it is not Einstein.

steps: Let $(M,g)$ have [constant curvature](c:constant-curvature) $K$, so every sectional curvature equals $K$.
The Ricci curvature of a unit vector is a sum of $n-1$ sectional curvatures, so $\mathrm{Ric}(v,v)=(n-1)K$.
Hence $\mathrm{Ric}(g)=(n-1)K\,g$, and $g$ is an Einstein metric.
The converse fails: the product of two unit $2$-spheres is Einstein but does not have constant curvature.
links.why: It shows that every metric of constant curvature is Einstein, and that Einstein metrics form a larger class.

reminder: An elementary function is built from constants, powers, exponentials, logarithms and trigonometric functions by arithmetic and composition.
definition: The elementary functions are the smallest class of functions of one complex variable that contains the identity, the constant functions, the power functions $x^\gamma$, the [exponential function](c:exponential-function), the [logarithm](c:logarithm) and the [trigonometric functions](c:trigonometric-function), and that is closed under sums, products, quotients and composition. Inverses of these, such as $\arcsin$, are elementary as well.
examples: $f(x)=\sin(x^2)+e^x/(1+x^2)$ is elementary.
$\arctan x$ and $\sqrt{x}$ are elementary.
Non-example: $\operatorname{erf}(x)=\frac2{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^xe^{-t^2}\,dt$ is not elementary, by a theorem of Liouville.

steps: Take a [rational function](c:rational-function) $p(x)/q(x)$ with polynomials $p$ and $q$.
A polynomial is built from the identity and constants by sums and products.
The quotient $p/q$ is built by one more quotient, which the elementary class allows.
So every rational function is elementary.
links.why: It shows that elementary functions include all rational functions and then add exponentials, logarithms and more.

reminder: An elementary group is a [direct product](c:direct-product) of a cyclic group and a $p$-group, with the cyclic order prime to $p$.
definition: A [finite group](c:finite-group) $H$ is $p$-elementary, for a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$, when $H$ is a [direct product](c:direct-product) $C\times P$ of a [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) $C$ of order prime to $p$ and a [p-group](c:p-group) $P$. It is elementary when it is $p$-elementary for some prime $p$.
examples: Every cyclic group is elementary: take $P$ trivial and $p$ a prime that does not divide the order.
Every $p$-group is elementary: take $C$ trivial.
The group $\mathbb{Z}/3\times(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ is $2$-elementary.
Non-example: $S_3$ is not elementary, because every group $C\times P$ of order $6$ is abelian while $S_3$ is not.

steps: Take a [p-group](c:p-group) $P$.
Write $P=C\times P$ with $C$ the trivial cyclic group, which has order prime to $p$.
So $P$ is $p$-elementary, hence elementary.
links.why: It shows that an elementary group is a $p$-group with an extra cyclic factor allowed.

steps: Let $H=C\times P$ be elementary, with $C$ cyclic and $P$ a $p$-group.
A cyclic group is abelian, so it is nilpotent.
Every finite $p$-group is nilpotent.
A direct product of nilpotent groups is nilpotent, so $H$ is a [nilpotent group](c:nilpotent-group).
links.why: It shows that elementary groups are nilpotent, so results on nilpotent groups apply to them.

reminder: An elementary row operation swaps two rows, scales a row by a nonzero number, or adds a multiple of one row to another.
definition: An elementary row operation changes a [matrix](c:matrix) over a [field](c:field) in one of three ways: swap two rows ($R_i\leftrightarrow R_j$), multiply one row by a nonzero scalar ($R_i\to cR_i$ with $c\ne0$), or add a multiple of one row to a different row ($R_i\to R_i+cR_j$ with $i\ne j$). Each operation is invertible, and it equals left multiplication by an [elementary matrix](c:elementary-matrix).
examples: Replacing $R_2$ by $R_2-3R_1$ is an elementary row operation.
Swapping the first and the third row is an elementary row operation.
Gaussian elimination reduces any matrix to row echelon form with a finite sequence of elementary row operations.
Non-example: replacing a row by $0$ times itself is not allowed, because the scalar must be nonzero and the operation must be invertible.

reminder: An elementary subgroup of a finite group $G$ is a subgroup of $G$ that is an [elementary group](c:elementary-group).
definition: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group). An elementary subgroup of $G$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H\le G$ that is an [elementary group](c:elementary-group): for some prime $p$, $H\cong C\times P$ with $C$ cyclic of order prime to $p$ and $P$ a $p$-group.
examples: In $S_3$, the subgroup generated by a $3$-cycle is elementary, because it is cyclic.
Every subgroup of a $p$-group is elementary, because it is again a $p$-group.
In $A_4$, the Klein four-group is an elementary subgroup, because it is a $2$-group.
Non-example: $S_3$ is not an elementary subgroup of itself, because $S_3$ is not an elementary group.

steps: Take a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H$ of a finite group $G$.
Add the condition that $H\cong C\times P$ with $C$ cyclic of order prime to $p$ and $P$ a $p$-group, for some prime $p$.
Then $H$ is an elementary subgroup of $G$.
links.why: It shows that an elementary subgroup is a subgroup with one extra condition on its structure.

reminder: An ellipsoid is the image of the unit [ball](c:ball) under an invertible [affine map](c:affine-map).
definition: An ellipsoid in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a set $E=\{x:(x-c)^\top A(x-c)\le1\}$ with a center $c\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and a [positive-definite matrix](c:positive-definite-matrix) $A$; its surface is where equality holds. Equivalently, $E=\{c+Mu:|u|\le1\}$ for an invertible matrix $M$, so $E$ is the image of the unit [ball](c:ball) under an invertible [affine map](c:affine-map) of [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space).
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^3$, the set $x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2+z^2/c^2\le1$ is an ellipsoid with semi-axes $a$, $b$, $c$.
A ball of radius $r$ is an ellipsoid with $A=r^{-2}I$.
Non-example: the solid cylinder $x^2+y^2\le1$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is not an ellipsoid, because it is unbounded and its matrix is only positive semidefinite.

steps: Start with the closed [ball](c:ball) of radius $r$ and center $c$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
It equals $\{x:(x-c)^\top(r^{-2}I)(x-c)\le1\}$.
The matrix $r^{-2}I$ is positive definite, so the ball is an ellipsoid.
A general ellipsoid allows other positive-definite matrices, which stretch the ball by different amounts along perpendicular axes.
links.why: It shows that an ellipsoid is a ball that is stretched by different amounts in different directions.

reminder: A smooth embedding is an [immersion](c:immersion-of-smooth-manifolds) that is also a homeomorphism onto its image.
definition: A smooth map $f:M\to N$ of [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) is an embedding when it is an [immersion](c:immersion-of-smooth-manifolds), so its differential is injective at every point, and an [embedding of topological spaces](c:embedding-of-topological-spaces), so it is a homeomorphism onto its image. Then $f(M)$ is an embedded [submanifold](c:submanifold) of $N$ that is diffeomorphic to $M$.
examples: The inclusion $S^n\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a smooth embedding.
The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ from $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a smooth embedding.
Non-example: the map $\mathbb{R}\to T^2$, $t\mapsto(e^{it},e^{i\sqrt2t})$, is an injective immersion but not an embedding, because its image is dense and has a different topology.
Non-example: $t\mapsto(t^2,t^3)$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not an embedding, because its derivative vanishes at $t=0$.

steps: Let $f:M\to N$ be a smooth embedding.
By definition, the differential of $f$ is injective at every point.
So $f$ is an [immersion](c:immersion-of-smooth-manifolds).
The embedding case adds that $f$ is a homeomorphism onto its image.
links.why: It shows what an embedding adds to an immersion: a homeomorphism onto the image.

steps: Let $f:M\to N$ be a smooth embedding.
A smooth map is continuous, so $f$ is continuous.
By definition, $f$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, so it is an [embedding of topological spaces](c:embedding-of-topological-spaces).
The smooth case adds that $f$ is smooth with injective differential.
links.why: It shows that a smooth embedding is a topological embedding with extra smooth structure.

reminder: A topological embedding is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) that is a homeomorphism onto its [image](c:image).
definition: A [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f:X\to Y$ is an embedding of topological spaces when it is injective and the bijection $X\to f(X)$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism), where the [image](c:image) $f(X)$ carries the [subspace topology](c:subspace-topology) of $Y$. Equivalently, $f$ is injective and every open set of $X$ is $f^{-1}(V)$ for some open set $V$ of $Y$.
examples: The inclusion of a subspace $A\subseteq Y$ is an embedding.
The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ from $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ is an embedding of the circle.
Non-example: $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ on $[0,2\pi)$ is a continuous injection onto the circle but not an embedding, because its inverse is not continuous at $(1,0)$.

steps: Start with an embedding $f:X\to Y$.
Add the condition that $f$ is surjective, so $f(X)=Y$.
Then $f$ is a homeomorphism from $X$ onto $Y$.
links.why: It shows that a homeomorphism is an embedding that is onto.

steps: Start with a topological embedding $f:M\to N$ between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold).
Add the condition that $f$ is smooth.
Add the condition that $f$ is an [immersion](c:immersion-of-smooth-manifolds).
Then $f$ is an [embedding of differentiable manifolds](c:embedding-of-differentiable-manifolds).
links.why: It shows that a smooth embedding is a topological embedding that is smooth and has injective differential.

reminder: The empirical distribution function $F_n(x)$ is the fraction of the $n$ sample values that are at most $x$.
definition: For a sample $X_1,\dots,X_n$ of [random variables](c:random-variable), the empirical distribution function is $F_n(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{X_i\le x\}$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. It is a right-continuous step function that rises from $0$ to $1$, with jumps of size $1/n$ at the sample values, counted with multiplicity, and it is the [distribution function](c:distribution-function) of the measure that puts mass $1/n$ on each sample value.
examples: For the sample $2,5,5$, $F_3(x)=0$ for $x<2$, $F_3(x)=1/3$ for $2\le x<5$, and $F_3(x)=1$ for $x\ge5$.
For independent samples from a distribution $F$, $F_n(x)\to F(x)$ almost surely for each $x$, and the convergence is uniform by the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem.
Non-example: the distribution function $F$ of a continuous distribution is not an empirical distribution function, because it has no jumps.

steps: Let $\mu_n$ be the average of the [Dirac measures](c:dirac-measure) at the sample values, so each value has mass $1/n$.
Then $\mu_n$ is a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$.
Its [distribution function](c:distribution-function) is $x\mapsto\mu_n((-\infty,x])$, which equals $F_n(x)$.
So $F_n$ is the distribution function of a random variable that is uniform on the sample.
links.why: It shows that the empirical distribution function is an ordinary distribution function, so general facts apply to it.

reminder: An endofunctor is a [functor](c:functor) from a [category](c:category) to itself.
definition: An endofunctor of a [category](c:category) $\mathcal C$ is a [functor](c:functor) $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal C$ whose source and target are the same category. It sends each object $X$ to an object $FX$ and each morphism $f:X\to Y$ to a morphism $Ff:FX\to FY$, and it preserves identities and composition. Endofunctors of $\mathcal C$ can be composed with each other, and the identity functor is the unit for composition.
examples: The power set functor $\mathcal P:\mathbf{Set}\to\mathbf{Set}$ sends a function $f$ to the image map $A\mapsto f(A)$.
The list functor on $\mathbf{Set}$ sends a set $X$ to the set of finite lists in $X$ and applies $f$ to each entry of a list.
Non-example: the forgetful functor $\mathbf{Grp}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is not an endofunctor, because its source and target categories differ.

steps: Let $F$ be an endofunctor of $\mathcal C$, so $F$ is a functor $\mathcal C\to\mathcal C$.
It preserves identities and composition, as every [functor](c:functor) does.
So $F$ is a functor, and the endofunctor case adds only that source and target are equal.
links.why: It shows that an endofunctor is a functor whose source equals its target.

steps: Start with an endofunctor $T$ of $\mathcal C$.
Add a [natural transformation](c:natural-transformation) $\eta:\mathrm{id}\to T$, the unit.
Add a natural transformation $\mu:T\circ T\to T$, the multiplication.
Require the unit laws and the associativity law for $\mu$, and then $(T,\eta,\mu)$ is a [monad](c:monad).
links.why: It shows that a monad is an endofunctor with a unit, a multiplication and three laws.

reminder: An epsilon-number is an [ordinal](c:ordinal) $\alpha$ with $\omega^\alpha=\alpha$.
definition: An $\varepsilon$-number is an [ordinal](c:ordinal) $\alpha$ that is a [fixed point](c:fixed-point) of the ordinal map $\xi\mapsto\omega^\xi$, that is, $\omega^\alpha=\alpha$, where $\omega$ is the first infinite ordinal. The $\varepsilon$-numbers form an increasing sequence $\varepsilon_0<\varepsilon_1<\varepsilon_2<\cdots$.
examples: $\varepsilon_0=\sup\{\omega,\omega^\omega,\omega^{\omega^\omega},\dots\}$ is the least $\varepsilon$-number, and $\omega^{\varepsilon_0}=\varepsilon_0$.
The next one, $\varepsilon_1$, is the supremum of $\varepsilon_0+1$, $\omega^{\varepsilon_0+1}$, $\omega^{\omega^{\varepsilon_0+1}}$ and so on.
Non-example: $\omega$ is not an $\varepsilon$-number, because $\omega^\omega>\omega$.

steps: Let $\alpha$ be an $\varepsilon$-number, so $\alpha$ is an [ordinal](c:ordinal).
The map $\xi\mapsto\omega^\xi$ sends ordinals to ordinals.
The epsilon case adds the condition $\omega^\alpha=\alpha$, so $\alpha$ is a fixed point of this map.
links.why: It shows that an epsilon-number is an ordinal with one extra condition, a fixed point of the map $\xi\mapsto\omega^\xi$.

reminder: The equivalence class of $x$ is the set of all elements related to $x$ by the [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation).
definition: Let $\sim$ be an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) on a [set](c:set) $X$. The equivalence class of $x\in X$ is $[x]=\{y\in X: y\sim x\}$. Two classes are equal or disjoint, so the classes partition $X$.
examples: For congruence modulo $3$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, $[1]=\{\dots,-5,-2,1,4,7,\dots\}$.
For a function $f:X\to Y$, the relation $x\sim x'$ when $f(x)=f(x')$ has the fibers of $f$ as its classes.
Two fractions $a/b$ and $c/d$ are equivalent when $ad=bc$, and a rational number is a class of fractions.
Non-example: for the relation $\le$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the set $\{y: y\le x\}$ is not an equivalence class, because $\le$ is not symmetric and these sets overlap.

steps: Let $H$ be a subgroup of a group $G$.
Define $x\sim y$ when $x^{-1}y\in H$; this is an equivalence relation.
The equivalence class of $x$ is $\{y: x^{-1}y\in H\}=xH$.
So every left [coset](c:coset) of $H$ is an equivalence class.
links.why: It shows that cosets are the equivalence classes of a relation defined by a subgroup, so facts on partitions apply to them.

reminder: Equivariant stable cohomotopy is the [equivariant cohomology](c:equivariant-cohomology) theory that the [equivariant sphere spectrum](c:equivariant-sphere-spectrum) represents.
definition: For a [compact Lie group](c:compact-lie-group) $G$, equivariant stable cohomotopy is the [equivariant cohomology](c:equivariant-cohomology) theory represented by the [equivariant sphere spectrum](c:equivariant-sphere-spectrum) $\mathbb{S}_G$. For a $G$-space $X$ and an integer $n$, $\pi^n_G(X)$ is the group of homotopy classes of $G$-maps of $G$-spectra from the suspension spectrum of $X_+$ to the $n$-fold suspension of $\mathbb{S}_G$.
examples: For the trivial group, it is the ordinary [stable cohomotopy](c:stable-cohomotopy) of spaces.
In degree $0$ the value on a point is the Burnside ring: $\pi^0_G(\mathrm{pt})\cong A(G)$ for a finite group $G$.
Non-example: the equivariant cohomotopy of $G$-maps $X\to S^n$ without stabilization is unstable and has no suspension isomorphism.

steps: Take the trivial group $G=1$.
A $1$-spectrum is an ordinary spectrum, and $\mathbb{S}_1$ is the ordinary sphere spectrum.
So $\pi^n_1(X)$ is the [stable cohomotopy](c:stable-cohomotopy) of $X$.
links.why: It shows that equivariant stable cohomotopy extends stable cohomotopy to spaces with a group action.

steps: An [equivariant cohomology](c:equivariant-cohomology) theory on $G$-spaces is represented by a $G$-spectrum $E$ through $E^n_G(X)=[X_+,\Sigma^nE]^G$.
Choose $E=\mathbb{S}_G$, the equivariant sphere spectrum.
The resulting theory is equivariant stable cohomotopy.
links.why: It shows that equivariant stable cohomotopy is the cohomology theory with the sphere spectrum as its representing object.

reminder: A $G$-map is an equivariant weak equivalence when it is a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence) on the fixed points of every closed subgroup.
definition: Let $G$ be a [topological group](c:topological-group). A $G$-equivariant map $f:X\to Y$ of $G$-spaces is an equivariant weak homotopy equivalence when, for every [closed subgroup](c:closed-subgroup) $H\le G$, the map $f^H:X^H\to Y^H$ of [fixed point spaces](c:fixed-point-space) is a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence). Equivalently, $f$ induces isomorphisms on all [equivariant homotopy groups](c:equivariant-homotopy-group).
examples: A $G$-homotopy equivalence is an equivariant weak homotopy equivalence.
For the trivial group $G$, the notion is the same as a weak homotopy equivalence.
Every $G$-space $X$ receives an equivariant weak homotopy equivalence from a $G$-CW complex, called a $G$-CW approximation.

Non-example: for $G=\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $EG=S^\infty$ with the antipodal action, the map $EG\to\mathrm{pt}$ is a weak homotopy equivalence but not an equivariant one, because $EG^G=\emptyset$ while $\mathrm{pt}^G=\mathrm{pt}$.

steps: Take the trivial group $G=\{e\}$.
Its only closed subgroup is $G$, and $X^G=X$.
So the condition says that $f:X\to Y$ is a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence).
links.why: It shows that the equivariant notion is the ordinary one tested on the fixed points of every subgroup.

reminder: An error-correcting code is a set of words that pairwise differ in many positions, so a few wrong symbols can be repaired.
definition: Let $A$ be a finite [set](c:set), the alphabet. A code of length $n$ is a [subset](c:subset) $C\subseteq A^n$ whose elements are the codewords. Its minimum distance $d$ is the least number of positions in which two different codewords differ, and the code corrects every pattern of up to $\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor$ wrong symbols by decoding to the nearest codeword.
examples: The repetition code $\{000,111\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^3$ has minimum distance $3$ and corrects one wrong bit.
The Hamming $(7,4)$ code has $16$ codewords of length $7$ and minimum distance $3$.
Non-example: all of $\{0,1\}^3$ has minimum distance $1$ and corrects no error, because a changed bit gives another word of the code.

steps: Take a [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_q$ as the alphabet.
Add the condition that the code is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$.
Then the code is a [linear code](c:linear-code), and its minimum distance is the least number of nonzero entries in a nonzero codeword.
links.why: It shows that a linear code is a code with algebraic structure, which makes its distance and decoding easier to compute.

reminder: An essentially algebraic theory has operations that are defined only where certain equations hold, and its axioms are equations.
definition: An essentially algebraic theory is a many-sorted [algebraic theory](c:algebraic-theory) in which some operations are [partial functions](c:partial-function). It has a set of total operation symbols, further operation symbols $\sigma$ that each come with a set of [equations](c:equation) in the total ones, and equational axioms. A model makes the total operations defined everywhere, makes $\sigma(\vec a)$ defined exactly where the equations of $\sigma$ hold, and satisfies each axiom wherever both of its sides are defined.
examples: The theory of categories has objects, morphisms, and a composite $g\circ f$ that is defined exactly when $\mathrm{dom}(g)=\mathrm{cod}(f)$.
The theory of groups, in which every operation is total, is an essentially algebraic theory.
Non-example: the theory of fields is not essentially algebraic, because $x^{-1}$ must be defined exactly when $x\ne0$, and $x\ne0$ is not an equation.

steps: Start with a many-sorted [algebraic theory](c:algebraic-theory), where every operation is total.
Declare every operation symbol to be total, so no domain equations are needed.
Then the models are the same as before, so the theory is essentially algebraic.
The general case adds operations whose domains are cut out by equations.
links.why: It shows that essentially algebraic theories include all algebraic theories and add partial operations.

reminder: The étale fundamental group of a connected [scheme](c:scheme) is the profinite group that classifies its finite étale covers.
definition: Let $X$ be a connected [scheme](c:scheme) with a [geometric point](c:geometric-point) $\bar x$. The [fiber functor](c:fiber-functor) sends a finite [étale cover](c:etale-cover) $Y\to X$ to the finite set of geometric points of $Y$ over $\bar x$. The étale fundamental group $\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(X,\bar x)$ is the group of automorphisms of this fiber functor, a [profinite group](c:profinite-group), and the fiber functor is an equivalence from finite étale covers of $X$ to finite sets with a continuous action of this group.
examples: For $X=\operatorname{Spec}k$ with $k$ a field, the étale fundamental group is the absolute Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(k^{\mathrm{sep}}/k)$.
For a connected complex variety of finite type, it is the profinite completion of the topological fundamental group; for $\mathbb{C}^\times$ it is $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}$.
Non-example: the topological fundamental group $\mathbb{Z}$ of the circle is not profinite, while the étale fundamental group of $\mathbb{C}^\times$ is its profinite completion $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}$.

steps: Take $X=\operatorname{Spec}k$ for a field $k$, with the geometric point given by a separable closure $k^{\mathrm{sep}}$.
Finite étale covers of $X$ are the spectra of finite étale $k$-algebras $A$.
The fiber functor sends such a cover to the finite set $\mathrm{Hom}_k(A,k^{\mathrm{sep}})$.
Its automorphism group is the [absolute Galois group](c:absolute-galois-group) $\mathrm{Gal}(k^{\mathrm{sep}}/k)$.
links.why: It shows that the étale fundamental group extends the absolute Galois group from fields to schemes.

reminder: A Euclidean domain is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain) with a size function that allows division with remainder.
definition: An [integral domain](c:integral-domain) $R$ is a Euclidean domain when there is a function $N$ from the nonzero elements of $R$ to the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) such that for all $a,b\in R$ with $b\ne0$ there are $q,r\in R$ with $a=bq+r$, and either $r=0$ or $N(r)<N(b)$. Such a function $N$ makes the Euclidean algorithm work in $R$, so it computes [greatest common divisors](c:greatest-common-divisor).
examples: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ with $N(n)=|n|$ form a Euclidean domain.
For a field $k$, the polynomial ring $k[x]$ with $N(f)=\deg f$ is a Euclidean domain.
The Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ with $N(a+bi)=a^2+b^2$ form a Euclidean domain.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is not a Euclidean domain, because the ideal $(2,x)$ is not principal.

steps: Let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of $R$ and pick $b\in I\setminus\{0\}$ with $N(b)$ minimal.
For $a\in I$, write $a=bq+r$ with $r=0$ or $N(r)<N(b)$.
Then $r=a-bq$ lies in $I$, so minimality forces $r=0$.
Hence $I=(b)$, so every ideal is principal and $R$ is a [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain).
links.why: It shows that every Euclidean domain is a principal ideal domain, so unique factorization holds in it.

reminder: An Euler circuit is a closed walk in a [graph](c:graph) that uses every edge exactly once.
definition: An Euler circuit of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ is a closed walk that starts and ends at the same [vertex](c:vertex) and traverses each [edge](c:edge) of $G$ exactly once. A connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree (Euler).
examples: The triangle $K_3$ has the Euler circuit $a\,b\,c\,a$.
The complete graph $K_5$ has an Euler circuit, because every vertex has degree $4$.
Non-example: the graph of the seven bridges of Königsberg has no Euler circuit, because all four of its vertices have odd degree.
Non-example: $K_4$ has no Euler circuit, because every vertex has odd degree $3$.

reminder: Excision lets one cut a small subspace $Z$ out of a pair $(X,A)$ without changing the relative [homology](c:homology).
definition: A homology theory $h_*$ satisfies excision when, for subsets $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) with the [closure](c:closure) of $Z$ inside the [interior](c:interior) of $A$, the inclusion $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)\to(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms $h_n(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)\to h_n(X,A)$ in [relative homology](c:relative-homology) for all $n$. Excision is one of the [Eilenberg-Steenrod axioms](c:eilenberg-steenrod-axioms).
examples: Singular homology satisfies excision, and this gives the [Mayer-Vietoris sequence](c:mayer-vietoris-sequence).
For a good pair $(X,A)$, excision gives $H_n(X,A)\cong\tilde H_n(X/A)$.
Non-example: the relative homotopy groups $\pi_n(X,A)$ do not satisfy excision in general; they satisfy it only in a range, which is the Blakers–Massey theorem.
